paragraphs.source_en: Dokusen now opened his mouth and said, “Whether one calls it intuition or sensation, at any rate it is certain that the freer a person’s individuality becomes, the more cramped life becomes. Nietzsche’s raising of the banner of the Superman was entirely because this cramped feeling had nowhere to go, and so it became distorted into that sort of philosophy. At first glance it looks like his ideal, but it is not; it is discontent. Crouched in the nineteenth century, when individuality had developed so far that one could not even turn over freely beside one’s neighbor, the fellow grew a little desperate and scribbled all that wild stuff. Reading what he wrote, rather than feeling exhilarated, one feels sorry for him. To me his voice never sounds like one of bold advance; it is a voice of resentment and passionate indignation. Nor is that surprising, for in ancient times, if one great man appeared, all under heaven gathered beneath his banner, which was a very pleasant thing. And when such pleasure actually existed, there was no need, as with Nietzsche, to display it in a book by the power of pen and paper. Thus Homer and the fifteenth-century English ballads, though they likewise depict superhuman characters, give an entirely different impression. They are cheerful. They are written in high spirits. Because there was actual pleasure, and that pleasant fact was transferred onto paper, naturally there is no bitter taste in it. Nietzsche’s age could not do that. Not a single heroic figure appeared, and even if one had appeared, no one would have set him up as a hero. In olden times there was only one Confucius, so Confucius carried weight; nowadays there are several Confuciuses, perhaps everyone is Confucius, so even if someone comes out and says, ‘I am Confucius,’ people are not impressed. Because people are not impressed, one becomes discontented oneself; and because one is discontented, one can only make a show of it in books. We desired freedom, and we obtained freedom; as a result of obtaining freedom, we keenly feel unfree and are at a loss what to do. That is why Western civilization, though it may look rather fine at first glance, is in the end no great thing. By contrast, in the East people have cultivated the heart from ancient times; that way is the right one. Look: as the result of the development of individuality, everyone has fallen into nervous exhaustion, and when no one knows how to manage it, only then do they begin to discover the value of the phrase ‘the people of a true king are broad and at ease,’ and to realize that ‘transforming without action’ is not a saying to be taken lightly. But even if they realize it, by then it is too late. It is very much like coming down with alcoholism and only then thinking how much better it would have been not to have drunk so wildly.”
